choice: Use a dissociative Langmuir–Hinshelwood/Temkin-like aggregate mechanism for plant transfer: N2 adsorption/dissociation, sequential N hydrogenation, NH3 desorption; retain catalyst-specific measured productivity as the activity anchor and represent equilibrium through the reaction quotient. Treat associative pathways reported for selected hydride/single-atom catalysts as contributors already embedded in their measured anchor rather than imposing a separate unidentifiable pathway on every catalyst.
alternatives: Universal associative N2 hydrogenation mechanism
Full catalyst-specific microkinetic model for every literature material
Empirical conversion-only model without a mechanistic equilibrium term
reason: The literature set spans Fe, Ru, Co, Ni, hydride/imide, nitride and carbon catalysts, but only a subset reports enough reaction orders or elementary-step data for catalyst-specific microkinetics. A common dissociative aggregate model preserves comparability and the mandatory thermodynamic direction while measured rates retain material-specific pathway advantages.

choice: Anchor intrinsic activity to each usable record's measured NH3 productivity and transfer it with an Arrhenius factor, a sublinear total-pressure factor, feed-composition correction, and reversible approach-to-equilibrium factor max(0,1-Q/K). Optimize plant per-pass conversion subject to equilibrium and the catalyst-throughput constraint. Apply observed 10%-activity lifetime when available; otherwise use a sourced catalyst-life assumption with uncertainty.
alternatives: Use laboratory conversion directly as plant per-pass conversion
Use a single published iron-catalyst rate equation for all catalyst classes
Assume rate independent of temperature, pressure and equilibrium
Fit catalyst-specific kinetic parameters despite sparse heterogeneous data
reason: Laboratory conversion is reactor/contact-time dependent and cannot be transported directly. Rate anchoring avoids inventing catalyst-specific prefactors, while reversible scaling captures the dominant plant effects—temperature, pressure, stoichiometry and equilibrium/recycle—using parameters that can be tested by sensitivity.

choice: Use a high-pressure multi-bed fixed-bed catalytic ammonia converter with interbed heat removal and adjustable loop pressure, reactor temperature, and per-pass N2 conversion; catalyst inventory is sized from transferred productivity and optimized jointly with recycle burden.
alternatives: Single adiabatic packed bed
Fluidized-bed reactor
Membrane reactor with in-situ NH3 removal
Once-through low-pressure reactor
reason: Industrial ammonia synthesis requires equilibrium management and heat removal for a strongly exothermic reversible reaction. Multiple fixed beds with cooling are mature, permit catalyst comparison on a common basis, and expose the conversion-versus-recycle tradeoff central to plant ranking.

choice: Cool the high-pressure reactor effluent and condense NH3, separate liquid product from unreacted N2/H2, recycle the gas, and purge a small fraction to control accumulated feed impurities; use refrigeration/cooling duty that varies with loop flow and conversion.
alternatives: Pressure-swing adsorption of NH3
Absorption in water or acid
Membrane separation
Once-through product recovery without recycle
reason: High-pressure condensation is compatible with the synthesis loop and directly couples low per-pass conversion to larger cooling, separator, and recycle-compression duties. Alternative separations would add unvalidated selectivity and material parameters across all catalysts.

choice: Battery limit begins with purified gaseous H2 and N2 at 298.15 K and 30 bar and ends with 99.8 mol% liquid NH3 at 20 bar; upstream H2 production and air separation are excluded, while all synthesis-loop compression, heating, reaction, cooling/condensation, recycle, purge handling, product letdown, and loop offsites are included.
alternatives: Include electrolysis and air separation
Begin with syngas from natural-gas reforming
End at hot reactor effluent
Include ammonia storage and export shipping
reason: The requested comparison concerns catalyst choice in ammonia synthesis. A purified-feed synthesis-loop boundary isolates catalyst-driven effects while retaining every unit whose duty changes with equilibrium, conversion, temperature, pressure, and recycle.

choice: Use a bottom-up annualized synthesis-loop cost in 2024 USD per tonne NH3: fixed-table H2 and electricity prices, catalyst replacement from inventory/life and fixed-table material prices, and unit-by-unit installed capital annualized by the fixed-table capital recovery factor plus fixed O&M. Scale each unit from the 600 kt/y reference and its own calculated duty/throughput; optimize operating temperature, pressure and per-pass conversion for each catalyst.
alternatives: Copy a published levelized ammonia cost
Apply one undifferentiated plant CAPEX factor to all catalysts
Ignore catalyst inventory and replacement cost
Use product selling price as a proxy for production cost
reason: The task requires every quoted cost to originate in this model and requires unit duties to respond to conversion, recycle and catalyst activity. Unit-level annualization preserves those couplings while fixed workspace prices ensure consistent comparisons.

choice: Use atomic nitrogen adsorption energy relative to 1/2 N2 as the descriptor; stronger binding is more negative. Represent dissociative N2 activation, dissociative H2 adsorption, and sequential N→NH→NH2→NH3 hydrogenation with linear adsorbate scaling and BEP barriers, producing a Sabatier volcano between N2 activation on weak-binding metals and hydrogenation/NH3 release on strong-binding metals.
alternatives: N2 dissociation barrier alone
Metal d-band center
Hydrogen adsorption energy
Catalyst-specific descriptors for every support and promoter
reason: Nitrogen binding directly captures the established ammonia-synthesis volcano across transition metals and can be connected to one thermodynamically consistent microkinetic network; support/promoter effects remain outside the one-descriptor backward-design scope.
